# Oat

<section class="hmi-quick-read" id="oat-quick-read" data-hmi-quick-read aria-labelledby="oat-quick-read-label"><div class="hmi-quick-read-label" id="oat-quick-read-label">Quick read</div>

<li>
<strong>Metals measured:</strong>

Lead, cadmium, total arsenic, inorganic arsenic, dimethylarsinic acid and total mercury and others, in 407 results from 25 sources.<sup class="cite">[[sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants|1]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">World Health Organization · 2026</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">GEMS/Food Contaminants database heavy-metal exports</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">GEMS/Food Contamination Monitoring and Assessment Programme</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">Read source →</a></span></span></sup><sup class="cite">[[sources/authors2025-evaluation-of-concentrations-and-health-risk-assessment-of|2]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Unknown authors · 2025</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/authors2025-evaluation-of-concentrations-and-health-risk-assessment-of">Evaluation of Concentrations and Health Risk Assessment of Cadmium, Lead, Chromium and Arsenic in</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Peer-reviewed article</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/authors2025-evaluation-of-concentrations-and-health-risk-assessment-of">Read source →</a></span></span></sup><sup class="cite">[[sources/begday2026-plant-milk-heavy-metal-safety|3]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Inna V. </li>
<li>
<strong>Main drivers:</strong>

Oat, as sold from retail brand A had lead higher at 2,800 µg/kg, against 1,100 µg/kg for retail brand A in the same study.<sup class="cite">[[sources/shaikh2025-mumbai-ready-to-eat-foods-voltammetry|7]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Shaikh U, Samant R · 2025</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/shaikh2025-mumbai-ready-to-eat-foods-voltammetry">Quantitative Determination of Heavy Metals in Ready to Eat Food Products</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">International Journal for Multidisciplinary Research (IJFMR) 7(6), November-December 2025</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/shaikh2025-mumbai-ready-to-eat-foods-voltammetry">Read source →</a></span></span></sup>

</li>
<li>
<strong>Practical framing:</strong>

Ask for lot results with a quantification limit well below the limit that applies in the destination market.<sup class="cite">[[sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants|1]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">World Health Organization · 2026</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">GEMS/Food Contaminants database heavy-metal exports</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">GEMS/Food Contamination Monitoring and Assessment Programme</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">Read source →</a></span></span></sup><sup class="cite">[[sources/authors2025-evaluation-of-concentrations-and-health-risk-assessment-of|2]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Unknown authors · 2025</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/authors2025-evaluation-of-concentrations-and-health-risk-assessment-of">Evaluation of Concentrations and Health Risk Assessment of Cadmium, Lead, Chromium and Arsenic in</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Peer-reviewed article</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/authors2025-evaluation-of-concentrations-and-health-risk-assessment-of">Read source →</a></span></span></sup><sup class="cite">[[sources/begday2026-plant-milk-heavy-metal-safety|3]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Inna V. <div class="hmi-analyte-explorer" id="hmi-occurrence-oat" data-analyte-explorer data-compact-intro="true" data-source-summaries="true"><details class="hmi-drawer-disclosure" data-explorer-context><summary data-open-context aria-haspopup="dialog" aria-controls="hmi-occurrence-oat-drawer">Comparison methods and scope</summary><div data-explorer-context-content>

<p>Each row is one statistic a source reports for one form of oat, group and metal; percentiles, ranges and maxima reported for the same samples as a mean or median are shown on that row. Different forms and preparation states are kept apart, and dry-weight results never share a reference with as-sold or fresh-weight results. Ratings place a result against an HMI reference built from monitoring results and ordinary-setting medians for the same form and basis. Same-study contrasts compare a contaminated or treated site with its control, targeted with random sampling, a prepared form with the unprocessed one, or one group of a study with the median of its other groups. Held rows failed a check against their own source and are shown but not compared.</p>

data-shared-occurrence-methods><summary>Shared dataset methods and interpretation</summary><div data-shared-evidence-content><p>Source summaries retain their original statistic, material, basis and censoring. Each source drawer identifies methods and overlapping samples. No matched reference or pooled distribution is inferred.</p></div></details><details class="hmi-drawer-disclosure" data-baseline-fallback id="hmi-reference-hmi-pooled-reference-v2:oat-fde3e777ae46:ed3744fc470c"><summary>HMI oat Pb reference · Oat, as sold</summary><div data-baseline-reference-template="hmi-pooled-reference-v2:oat-fde3e777ae46:ed3744fc470c"><p class="hmi-drawer-section-title" role="heading" aria-level="3">Reference and scope</p><p>HMI oat Pb reference · Oat, as sold. Oat, as sold; As sold, as eaten or fresh weight, µg/kg; no moisture conversion. Distribution of subgroup median concentration values.</p><div class="hmi-drawer-table"><table><thead><tr><th scope="col">Reference (µg/kg)</th><th scope="col">Q1</th><th scope="col">Median</th><th scope="col">Q3</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><td>Primary HMI reference</td><td>3.7–14 (bounded)</td><td>20–47.7 (bounded)</td><td>135–170 (bounded)</td></tr><tr><td>Alternative weighting</td><td>4–11.5 (bounded)</td><td>20–47.7 (bounded)</td><td>135–170 (bounded)</td></tr></tbody></table></div><p>103 reference units; 6 sampling families. Counts describe evidence units, not independent studies or certainty.</p><div class="hmi-drawer-table"><table><thead><tr><th scope="col">Contributing family</th><th scope="col">Reference units</th><th scope="col">Weight</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><td>WHO GEMS/Food</td><td>87</td><td>17%</td></tr><tr><td>authors 2025</td><td>1</td><td>17%</td></tr><tr><td>Bielecka et al. 2022</td><td>1</td><td>17%</td></tr><tr><td>Marques et al. 2021</td><td>2</td><td>17%</td></tr><tr><td>Shaikh et al. 2025</td><td>3</td><td>17%</td></tr><tr><td>U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2024</td><td>9</td><td>17%</td></tr></tbody></table></div><p class="hmi-drawer-section-title" role="heading" aria-level="3">Methods</p><p>HMI pools subgroup medians for oat, as sold on a as sold, as eaten or fresh weight basis: monitoring results summarized as one median per reporting region, sampling type and collection year, total diet composites and printed sample values as single observations, and printed subgroup medians from ordinary farms or markets. Each sampling family has equal total weight. Non-detects stay as zero-to-limit intervals, so quartiles carry lower and upper bounds. Means, ranges and maxima never enter as observations. Other forms, other bases, targeted sampling and results from mining, industrial, wastewater-affected, experimental, fertiliser or manufacturer settings are kept out of this reference.</p><p>Inverse weighted empirical CDF; midpoint at exact cumulative-weight boundaries. At least four reference units and a definitely positive Q1 to Q3 spread are required. This is a display eligibility rule, not statistical validation.</p><p class="hmi-drawer-section-title" role="heading" aria-level="3">Limitations</p><p>6 sampling families with different designs; none is a probability sample of world supply. Reporting regions and purchase markets are not growing areas. Non-detects with differing limits widen the bounds. Each sampling family has equal total weight. Non-detects stay as zero-to-limit intervals, so quartiles carry lower and upper bounds. Means, ranges and maxima never enter as observations. This is a display eligibility rule, not statistical validation.</p><p class="hmi-drawer-section-title" role="heading" aria-level="3">Limitations</p><p>Marques et al. 2021 is the only compatible sampling family for oat, as sold on this basis in the completed oat ledger, so this single-family reference cannot represent other markets. Reporting regions and purchase markets are not growing areas. Non-detects with differing limits widen the bounds. <a id="sources-and-contamination-pathways"></a>
## How metals reach oat

<a id="hmi-ing-010"></a>
<a id="what-evidence-supports-root-uptake-surface-deposition-feed-transfer-or-other-biological-pathways"></a>
<a id="hmi-ing-011"></a>
<a id="what-contamination-can-arise-from-agricultural-inputs-harvesting-processing-equipment-or-packaging"></a>
<a id="hmi-ing-012"></a>
<a id="which-source-attribution-claims-are-measured-modelled-inferred-or-unresolved"></a>

The evidence on how metals reach oat comes from studies that compared exposed and ordinary settings. Oat, as sold from retail brand A had lead higher at 2,800 µg/kg, against 1,100 µg/kg for retail brand A in the same study.<sup class="cite">[[sources/shaikh2025-mumbai-ready-to-eat-foods-voltammetry|7]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Shaikh U, Samant R · 2025</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/shaikh2025-mumbai-ready-to-eat-foods-voltammetry">Quantitative Determination of Heavy Metals in Ready to Eat Food Products</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">International Journal for Multidisciplinary Research (IJFMR) 7(6), November-December 2025</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/shaikh2025-mumbai-ready-to-eat-foods-voltammetry">Read source →</a></span></span></sup>

These are observational comparisons from single studies; the size of the difference depends on the site, metal and distance.

## Processing, cooking and preparation

<a id="hmi-ing-016"></a>
<a id="how-do-specified-processing-or-preparation-steps-change-the-measured-metal-endpoints"></a>
<a id="hmi-ing-017"></a>
<a id="how-do-derivatives-concentrates-extracts-and-fractions-differ-from-their-parent-ingredient"></a>
<a id="hmi-ing-018"></a>
<a id="do-changes-reflect-removal-redistribution-moisture-or-yield-change-dilution-or-altered-species-or-availability"></a>

Processed or prepared forms were compared only with unprocessed oat in the same study and group. Oat, flour or meal (product subgroup) had lead higher at 55.4 µg/kg, against 47.7 µg/kg for the unprocessed form in the same group (oat, as sold).<sup class="cite">[[sources/bielecka2022-poland-gluten-free-cereals-metals|4]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Bielecka J, Markiewicz-Żukowska R, Puścion-Jakubik A, Grabia M, Nowakowski P, Soroczyńska J, Socha K · 2022</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/bielecka2022-poland-gluten-free-cereals-metals">Gluten-Free Cereals and Pseudocereals as a Potential Source of Exposure to Toxic Elements among Polish Residents</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Nutrients 2022, 14, 2342</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/bielecka2022-poland-gluten-free-cereals-metals">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> In another study, oat, cooked (EURO) had cadmium higher at 35 µg/kg, against 15 µg/kg for the unprocessed form in the same group (oat, as sold).<sup class="cite">[[sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants|1]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">World Health Organization · 2026</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">GEMS/Food Contaminants database heavy-metal exports</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">GEMS/Food Contamination Monitoring and Assessment Programme</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">Read source →</a></span></span></sup>

Forms differ in water content, so a per-kilogram difference is not by itself a measured removal or gain of metal.



<a id="mitigation-options"></a>
## Mitigation for oat

<a id="hmi-ing-019"></a>
<a id="which-prevention-mitigation-or-remediation-measures-have-been-evaluated-for-this-ingredient"></a>
<a id="hmi-ing-020"></a>
<a id="under-what-conditions-at-which-stage-and-against-which-comparator-do-they-work-or-fail"></a>
<a id="hmi-ing-021"></a>
<a id="what-evidence-supports-field-or-commercial-implementation-and-ongoing-verification"></a>

Lot testing against the applicable limit is the check that can be verified.

<p class="hmi-mitigation-gap" data-mitigation-gap>No measured way to lower metals in this food is in the library yet.</p>



<a id="trade-offs-and-failure-modes"></a>
## Trade-offs and limits of controls

<a id="hmi-ing-022"></a>
<a id="can-an-intervention-increase-another-contaminant-or-redistribute-contamination-to-a-by-product"></a>
<a id="hmi-ing-023"></a>
<a id="what-effects-on-nutrition-yield-sensory-quality-stability-and-waste-streams-were-measured"></a>
<a id="hmi-ing-024"></a>
<a id="what-costs-constraints-adverse-effects-or-failure-modes-are-documented-and-which-are-unknown"></a>

Avoiding exposed growing areas lowered the metal measured in the studies available, but no study measured the cost or supply effect of doing so.<sup class="cite">[[sources/shaikh2025-mumbai-ready-to-eat-foods-voltammetry|7]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Shaikh U, Samant R · 2025</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/shaikh2025-mumbai-ready-to-eat-foods-voltammetry">Quantitative Determination of Heavy Metals in Ready to Eat Food Products</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">International Journal for Multidisciplinary Research (IJFMR) 7(6), November-December 2025</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/shaikh2025-mumbai-ready-to-eat-foods-voltammetry">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> Metals do not move together, so a lot that passes a lead limit says little about cadmium, arsenic or nickel unless those are tested as well.



<a id="sampling-and-testing"></a>
## Testing oat for metals

<a id="hmi-ing-025"></a>
<a id="what-sampling-design-is-appropriate-for-the-ingredient-heterogeneity-lot-and-decision"></a>
<a id="hmi-ing-026"></a>
<a id="which-methods-species-measurements-validation-evidence-and-reporting-limits-are-needed"></a>
<a id="hmi-ing-027"></a>
<a id="what-can-a-certificate-of-analysis-or-non-detect-establish-and-what-remains-untested"></a>

Results depend on the method and its reporting limit. Reporting limits for lead ranged from 1 µg/kg (WHO GEMS/Food) to 200 µg/kg (WHO GEMS/Food), so a non-detect from a less sensitive method says much less.<sup class="cite">[[sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants|1]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">World Health Organization · 2026</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">GEMS/Food Contaminants database heavy-metal exports</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">GEMS/Food Contamination Monitoring and Assessment Programme</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> Reporting limits for cadmium ranged from 0.7 µg/kg (WHO GEMS/Food) to 100 µg/kg (WHO GEMS/Food), so a non-detect from a less sensitive method says much less.<sup class="cite">[[sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants|1]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">World Health Organization · 2026</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">GEMS/Food Contaminants database heavy-metal exports</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">GEMS/Food Contamination Monitoring and Assessment Programme</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> Reporting limits for total arsenic ranged from 0.019 µg/kg (Bielecka et al. 2022) to 1,000 µg/kg (WHO GEMS/Food), so a non-detect from a less sensitive method says much less.<sup class="cite">[[sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants|1]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">World Health Organization · 2026</span><a →</a></span></span></sup><sup class="cite">[[sources/bielecka2022-poland-gluten-free-cereals-metals|4]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Bielecka J, →</a></span></span></sup>

A useful lot result names the form, the basis and a quantification limit well below the limit that applies.

<a id="universal-faqs"></a>
## Oat FAQs

<details class="qa" data-hmi-faq="1" id="what-heavy-metals-are-found-in-oat" data-anchor="what-heavy-metals-are-found-in-oat" data-question="What heavy metals are found in oat?">
<summary><span class="mk" aria-hidden="true"></span>What heavy metals are found in oat?</summary>
<div class="ans" data-hmi-faq-answer="1">

The library reports lead, cadmium, total arsenic, inorganic arsenic, dimethylarsinic acid, total mercury, nickel, chromium, tin, uranium, Co, Cu, Fe, Mn, Zn, V, Ca, Hg, Mg, Na and P in oat, most often lead, cadmium and total arsenic.<sup class="cite">[[sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants|1]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">World Health Organization · 2026</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">GEMS/Food Contaminants database heavy-metal exports</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">GEMS/Food Contamination Monitoring and Assessment Programme</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">Read source →</a></span></span></sup><sup class="cite">[[sources/authors2025-evaluation-of-concentrations-and-health-risk-assessment-of|2]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Unknown authors · 2025</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/authors2025-evaluation-of-concentrations-and-health-risk-assessment-of">Evaluation of Concentrations and Health Risk Assessment of Cadmium, Lead, Chromium and Arsenic in</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Peer-reviewed article</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/authors2025-evaluation-of-concentrations-and-health-risk-assessment-of">Read source →</a></span></span></sup><sup class="cite">[[sources/begday2026-plant-milk-heavy-metal-safety|3]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Inna V. Begday, Tamara A. Tsesar, Konstantin V. Kharin · 2026</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/begday2026-plant-milk-heavy-metal-safety">Integral assessment of the environmental safety of plant-based milk alternatives based on heavy metal analysis</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Izvestiya KGTU (KSTU News)</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/begday2026-plant-milk-heavy-metal-safety">Read source →</a></span></span></sup><sup class="cite">[[sources/bielecka2022-poland-gluten-free-cereals-metals|4]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Bielecka J, Markiewicz-Żukowska R, Puścion-Jakubik A, Grabia M, Nowakowski P, Soroczyńska J, Socha K · 2022</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/bielecka2022-poland-gluten-free-cereals-metals">Gluten-Free Cereals and Pseudocereals as a Potential Source of Exposure to Toxic Elements among Polish Residents</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Nutrients 2022, 14, 2342</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/bielecka2022-poland-gluten-free-cereals-metals">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> WHO GEMS/Food submissions reported lead in oat, as sold from 1,272 results in 3 reporting regions, with a subgroup median of 10 µg/kg.<sup class="cite">[[sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants|1]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">World Health Organization · 2026</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">GEMS/Food Contaminants database heavy-metal exports</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">GEMS/Food Contamination Monitoring and Assessment Programme</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">Read source →</a></span></span></sup>

</div>
</details>

<details class="qa" data-hmi-faq="1" id="how-do-heavy-metals-get-into-oat" data-anchor="how-do-heavy-metals-get-into-oat" data-question="How do heavy metals get into oat?">
<summary><span class="mk" aria-hidden="true"></span>How do heavy metals get into oat?</summary>
<div class="ans" data-hmi-faq-answer="1">

In the studies available, oat from contaminated or exposed settings carried more metal than oat from the same study’s control.<sup class="cite">[[sources/shaikh2025-mumbai-ready-to-eat-foods-voltammetry|7]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Shaikh U, Samant R · 2025</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/shaikh2025-mumbai-ready-to-eat-foods-voltammetry">Quantitative Determination of Heavy Metals in Ready to Eat Food Products</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">International Journal for Multidisciplinary Research (IJFMR) 7(6), November-December 2025</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/shaikh2025-mumbai-ready-to-eat-foods-voltammetry">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> Oat, as sold from retail brand A had lead higher at 2,800 µg/kg, against 1,100 µg/kg for retail brand A in the same study.<sup class="cite">[[sources/shaikh2025-mumbai-ready-to-eat-foods-voltammetry|7]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Shaikh U, Samant R · 2025</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/shaikh2025-mumbai-ready-to-eat-foods-voltammetry">Quantitative Determination of Heavy Metals in Ready to Eat Food Products</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">International Journal for Multidisciplinary Research (IJFMR) 7(6), November-December 2025</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/shaikh2025-mumbai-ready-to-eat-foods-voltammetry">Read source →</a></span></span></sup>

</div>
</details>

<details class="qa" data-hmi-faq="1" id="which-regions-report-the-lowest-levels-in-oat" data-anchor="which-regions-report-the-lowest-levels-in-oat" data-question="Which regions report the lowest levels in oat?">
<summary><span class="mk" aria-hidden="true"></span>Which regions report the lowest levels in oat?</summary>
<div class="ans" data-hmi-faq-answer="1">

Among GEMS/Food reporting regions, oat, as sold had the lowest cadmium subgroup median in PAHO (6.9 µg/kg) and the highest in EURO (100 µg/kg); reporting regions are markets, not growing areas.<sup class="cite">[[sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants|1]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">World Health Organization · 2026</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">GEMS/Food Contaminants database heavy-metal exports</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">GEMS/Food Contamination Monitoring and Assessment Programme</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> For inorganic arsenic, the lowest regional median was in PAHO (10.3 µg/kg) and the highest in WPRO (230 µg/kg).<sup class="cite">[[sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants|1]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">World Health Organization · 2026</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">GEMS/Food Contaminants database heavy-metal exports</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">GEMS/Food Contamination Monitoring and Assessment Programme</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">Read source →</a></span></span></sup>

</div>
</details>

<details class="qa" data-hmi-faq="1" id="does-processing-change-heavy-metals-in-oat" data-anchor="does-processing-change-heavy-metals-in-oat" data-question="Does processing change heavy metals in oat?">
<summary><span class="mk" aria-hidden="true"></span>Does processing change heavy metals in oat?</summary>
<div class="ans" data-hmi-faq-answer="1">

Only comparisons between forms in the same study are available, not before-and-after measurements of the same oat.<sup class="cite">[[sources/bielecka2022-poland-gluten-free-cereals-metals|4]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Bielecka J, Markiewicz-Żukowska R, Puścion-Jakubik A, Grabia M, Nowakowski P, Soroczyńska J, Socha K · 2022</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/bielecka2022-poland-gluten-free-cereals-metals">Gluten-Free Cereals and Pseudocereals as a Potential Source of Exposure to Toxic Elements among Polish Residents</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Nutrients 2022, 14, 2342</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/bielecka2022-poland-gluten-free-cereals-metals">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> Oat, flour or meal (product subgroup) had lead higher at 55.4 µg/kg, against 47.7 µg/kg for the unprocessed form in the same group (oat, as sold).<sup class="cite">[[sources/bielecka2022-poland-gluten-free-cereals-metals|4]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Bielecka J, Markiewicz-Żukowska R, Puścion-Jakubik A, Grabia M, Nowakowski P, Soroczyńska J, Socha K · 2022</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/bielecka2022-poland-gluten-free-cereals-metals">Gluten-Free Cereals and Pseudocereals as a Potential Source of Exposure to Toxic Elements among Polish Residents</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Nutrients 2022, 14, 2342</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/bielecka2022-poland-gluten-free-cereals-metals">Read source →</a></span></span></sup>

</div>
</details>

<details class="qa" data-hmi-faq="1" id="how-much-of-the-arsenic-in-oat-is-inorganic" data-anchor="how-much-of-the-arsenic-in-oat-is-inorganic" data-question="How much of the arsenic in oat is inorganic?">
<summary><span class="mk" aria-hidden="true"></span>How much of the arsenic in oat is inorganic?</summary>
<div class="ans" data-hmi-faq-answer="1">

Inorganic arsenic, the more toxic form, was measured in 13 results from 2 sources, far fewer than total arsenic.<sup class="cite">[[sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants|1]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">World Health Organization · 2026</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">GEMS/Food Contaminants database heavy-metal exports</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">GEMS/Food Contamination Monitoring and Assessment Programme</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">Read source →</a></span></span></sup><sup class="cite">[[sources/efsa2014-dietary-exposure-iAs|13]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">European Food Safety Authority (EFSA) · 2014</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/efsa2014-dietary-exposure-iAs">Dietary exposure to inorganic arsenic in the European population</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">EFSA Journal 2014;12(3):3597</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/efsa2014-dietary-exposure-iAs">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> European Food Safety Authority (EFSA) 2014 reported inorganic arsenic at 14.2 µg/kg (mean) in oat, as sold from European dietary-survey occurrence data.<sup class="cite">[[sources/efsa2014-dietary-exposure-iAs|13]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">European Food Safety Authority (EFSA) · 2014</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/efsa2014-dietary-exposure-iAs">Dietary exposure to inorganic arsenic in the European population</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">EFSA Journal 2014;12(3):3597</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/efsa2014-dietary-exposure-iAs">Read source →</a></span></span></sup>

</div>
</details>
